newsitem.title: GERMANY: EMU delay would mean flood of claims - De Silguy.
newsitem.headline: EMU delay would mean flood of claims - De Silguy.

text.p: European Commissioner Yves-Thibault de Silguy has raised the prospect of a flood of compensation claims from banks and big business in the event of a delay to Europe's planned single currency.

De Silguy's warning came as German Finance Minister Theo Waigel insisted Bonn was not discussing a delay, despite calls from within Chancellor Helmut Kohl's coalition to consider a postponement if France fails to qualify for the project.

"If the heads of government decide that we won't start until 2001 or 2002, then a flood of compensation claims will break out above us," De Silguy said in an interview to be published in Monday's edition of the German news magazine Der Spiegel.
"All the banks and companies who have trusted the treaty could demand the costs of their preparations back." said De Silguy, the EU's commissioner for monetary affairs.

De Silguy sidestepped direct questions about whether France could participate but hinted he favoured a strict interpretation of the budget deficit criterion in the Maastricht Treaty, which lays down the rules for economic and monetary union (EMU).
De Silguy said a decision to delay EMU would constitute a breach of international law, as the treaty lays down a start date of January 1, 1999.
He said this meant the European Union would also face charges of breaking the terms of the treaty in Europe's highest courts if heads of government decided to postpone the project.

Pressed on whether France could take part in EMU with a deficit of 3.5 percent of gross domestic product, he replied: "Confidence in the euro must be secured from the beginning. We can't take any risks when it comes to sticking to the criteria."

The treaty sets a target of three percent of GDP. As independent economists have raised doubts about whether France can achieve a figure of 3.0 by the end of the year, a debate is raging about whether the target can be interpreted more loosely.

Waigel said at a conference of his Christian Social Union party on Saturday that a postponement was not on the cards. "We're not conducting any debate about a delay," he said in the south German town of Trossenfurt.

Wolfgang Schaeuble, the powerful parliamentary leader of Kohl's Christian Democrats, said he was against a discussion about the figure behind the decimal point and that lasting stability of the euro was the most important consideration.

"France knows it must put everything into meeting the criteria in the Maastricht Treaty as a European currency must be supported by the confidence of the people and the markets," Schaeuble told Sunday's edition of the Bild am Sonntag weekly.
"But we must not play the role of a censor in French domestic policy," he added.
De Silguy said he thought even 3.0 was a high deficit level.

"In the case of France, that means the state spends 20 percent more than it takes in. The goal in Europe must be to achieve balanced budgets by the year 2002, following the role model of the United States," he said.
He made clear any delay would spell the end of economic monetary union.
"Then the euro is dead. For a new date after 1999, the treaty would have to be changed, with the whole procedure of ratification in the parliaments of the member states."
He said he was sure the euro would be launched on time.
"The debate about a postponement is unrealistic and dangerous. It's in the interests of Europe, France and Germany to have a common currency from 1999," he said.
